description: Gastrulation requires that epiblast cells in the primitive streak stop behaving as an epithelium and leave it, and this epithelial-mesenchymal transition is how mesoderm is generated; an incomplete version of the same programme delivers definitive endoderm. Posterior signals, prominently FGF acting through FGFR1 along with WNT, NODAL and BMP, converge on the primitive streak transcription factors EOMES and TBXT, which switch on SNAI1. SNAI1 then represses the genes that hold the epithelium together, including E-cadherin, occludin and claudins, so that junctions dissolve, cells detach from the basement membrane and ingress, and a mesenchymal expression programme with N-cadherin takes over. Without it the germ layers cannot be laid down. The same transcriptional switch is redeployed in carcinoma cells, where TGF-beta-driven loss of E-cadherin underlies invasion and metastasis, making this early developmental step a template for tumour cell dissemination.

After fertilization the embryo must erase the chromatin states it inherited from egg and sperm and build one capable of supporting its own transcription; these chromatin modifications during the maternal to zygotic transition accomplish that reprogramming. Both pronuclei lose DNA methylation, by different routes: in the paternal genome cytosine deamination and base excision repair, aided by TET3-mediated oxidation of 5-methylcytosine, replace modified bases with unmodified cytosine, while in the maternal genome DPPA3 blocks TET3 recruitment and displaces UHRF1 so that DNMT1-dependent maintenance methylation fails and demethylation occurs passively through cleavage divisions. In parallel, histone demethylases of the KDM5 and KDM6 families trim inherited H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, opening developmental loci. The result is the progressively accessible chromatin that permits zygotic genome activation, before methylation and repressive marks are re-imposed around implantation; failure impairs preimplantation development and imprint handling.

During gastrulation the primitive streak produces mesodermal subsets with distinct fates, and the lateral plate mesoderm is the population that goes on to build heart, limbs, blood, and the linings of the body cavity and gut. Its induction depends on Hedgehog signals, SHH and IHH, arriving from the adjacent endoderm to switch on the forkhead factor FOXF1, which marks the tissue once specified. FOXF1 then drives BMP4 expression, and BMP4 with FOXF1 turns on GATA4; BMP4 sustains FOXF1 while GATA4 reinforces its own transcription and that of BMP4, creating a self-maintaining loop that locks in lateral identity before downstream differentiation genes are engaged. Because this territory gives rise to cardiac and vascular progenitors, disturbance of the loop underlies congenital heart and diaphragm defects, and the same signals are used to derive these lineages from pluripotent stem cells.

Early in gastrulation, cells ingressing at the anterior primitive streak form the axial mesoderm, or chordamesoderm, the midline tissue that becomes the prechordal plate, head process and notochord. This midline is the embryo's organizing rod: it stiffens the body axis, patterns neural tube and somites through secreted Sonic Hedgehog, and later persists as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc, whose degeneration underlies disc disease. NODAL signalling through SMAD2 and SMAD3 cooperates with the pioneer factor FOXH1, with TEAD factors and their coactivator YAP1 released from Hippo restraint, and with the mesodermal factor TBXT to switch on FOXA2, which in turn drives notochord genes such as NOTO and SHH. WNT input via CTNNB1 with LEF1 and TCF7 positions this programme along the axis, coupling germ layer specification to midline identity.

The melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, in its melanocyte-specific M isoform, does more than drive pigmentation genes: it also sets how much oxidative metabolism a melanocyte or melanoma cell runs. By inducing PPARGC1A, the coactivator that coordinates mitochondrial biogenesis and respiratory gene expression, MITF pushes cells toward oxidative phosphorylation rather than glycolysis, and this axis helps explain why some melanomas survive targeted BRAF inhibition while low-MITF, low-PPARGC1A tumours are more invasive and drug-tolerant. MITF also raises expression of SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase that couples metabolic state to transcription and, through deacetylation of substrates including the p300 acetyltransferase, supports proliferation and opposes senescence. Together these targets make MITF a node linking lineage identity to cellular energetics, oxidative stress tolerance and melanoma phenotype switching.

Melanocytes depend on the transcription factor MITF-M not only to build pigment but to stay alive, and this branch of its output is the survival programme: MITF drives anti-apoptotic targets including BCL2, BCL2A1 and the IAP family member BIRC7, so melanoblasts survive migration and colonisation of the skin during development and melanocytes persist afterwards. Loss of this activity causes pigment cell death and depigmentation phenotypes, while its persistence in melanoma supports tumour cell survival and resistance to therapy. MITF also induces DICER1, linking it to microRNA processing, and one of its own targets, the TRPM1 intronic microRNA miR-211, acts with Argonaute proteins and TNRC6 scaffolds in silencing complexes to shape downstream gene expression. Repressive input comes through POU3F2 and the SIN3A-HDAC1 corepressor, tuning how much survival signal the lineage receives.

In melanocytes and melanoma cells the transcription factor MITF-M controls pigmentation and proliferation, but it also acts as a direct repressor of genes governing extracellular matrix organization, focal adhesion and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and this arm of its programme sets whether a cell proliferates or switches to an invasive, drug-resistant state. Loss or lowering of MITF-M releases adhesion and matrix targets such as the integrin subunit ITGA2, the focal adhesion scaffold paxillin, the matrix components EDIL3 and peroxidasin, and the plasminogen activator inhibitor SERPINE1, alongside phenotype-switch regulators including ZEB1, SOX2 and the cadherin pair CDH1 and CDH2. The result is cytoskeletal remodelling, altered attachment to matrix and a mesenchymal-like, migratory character. Because high MITF-M marks proliferative melanoma and low MITF-M marks quiescent invasive cells, this repressive output links a lineage transcription factor to metastatic behaviour and to resistance against targeted therapy.

Milk-secreting alveolar cells arise during pregnancy from hormone receptor-negative luminal progenitors of the mammary gland, the alternative fate to the ductal epithelium that lines the gland's branching ducts. This lineage decision is what allows lactation: without alveolar commitment and expansion there is no secretory compartment to synthesise and release milk. Fate choice is set by the interplay of Notch, WNT and hormone receptor signalling, with loss of Notch input pushing progenitors toward alveolar identity, and prolactin acting through its receptor and downstream STAT signalling to drive alveolar differentiation and milk protein production. Neighbouring myoepithelial cells contribute by modulating Notch ligand availability. After weaning, most alveolar cells are cleared by involution, but a surviving pool of alveolar precursors self-renews and reconstitutes the secretory tissue in later pregnancies, linking this programme to mammary stem cell hierarchy and to breast cancer subtype origins.

The basal layer of the mammary epithelium supplies its own committed progenitors, and the myoepithelial lineage arising from them gives the gland its contractile capacity: spindle-shaped cells wrapped around ducts and alveoli that squeeze milk toward the nipple in response to oxytocin, so that lactation fails without them. These cells sit between luminal cells and the basement membrane, which they help deposit, and their continuous sheath also acts as a barrier restraining luminal outgrowth. Specification toward this fate is driven by strong EGF receptor stimulation, and the ligands represented here — amphiregulin, EGF and TGF-alpha — are the inputs that set that signal intensity during ductal morphogenesis and organoid differentiation. Myoepithelial progenitors are normally unipotent, but after loss of luminal cells, EGFR together with Notch and Wnt signalling licenses them to regenerate the luminal compartment.

The earliest step in building a brain is the specification of the anterior neural plate, the rostral epiblast territory that will fold into a neural tube and give rise to forebrain and midbrain; failure of neural tube closure produces spina bifida and related congenital defects of the central nervous system. Anterior character depends on BMP signalling being held off by inhibitors from the anterior visceral endoderm, after which OTX2, ZIC2 and POU-domain factors including POU3F1 and POU5F1 act on an upstream enhancer to switch on SOX2 in the neuroepithelium. SOX1, PAX6, ZEB2 and ZNF521 accompany this transition from pluripotency, as NANOG and POU5F1 expression is resolved. The sharp limit with the posterior neural plate is set by reciprocal repression between high anterior OTX2 and posterior GBX2, fixing the midbrain-hindbrain boundary and the regional identity of later brain development.

An oocyte enters fertilization loaded with transcripts it made during oogenesis, and clearing them on schedule is what allows the embryo to switch from maternal to its own gene products. M-decay is the arm of this clearance carried out by factors the mother already stored in the egg, as opposed to later degradation driven by zygotic products; when it fails, oocytes arrest, zygotes stall at early cleavage and fertility is lost. Two adaptors set the timing: ZFP36L2 acts in the maturing oocyte and BTG4 after fertilization, each recruiting the multisubunit CCR4-NOT deadenylase, whose CNOT7/CNOT8 and CNOT6/CNOT6L nucleases shorten poly(A) tails and commit messages to decay. BTG4 links the complex to poly(A)-binding protein and the eIF4 cap-binding machinery, coupling translation to turnover. In parallel, DICER1-derived endogenous siRNAs guide AGO2 to slice complementary maternal mRNAs. Oocyte-specific factors such as NOBOX, ZP2 and PADI6 mark the transcripts and cellular context involved.

The embryo begins life transcriptionally silent, relying on maternal mRNA and protein; zygotic genome activation is the switch by which the newly formed embryonic genome starts transcribing for itself, and without it development arrests within the first few cleavages. It follows extensive epigenetic remodelling of both pronuclei, including DNA demethylation and changes in histone methylation and acetylation, and proceeds in a minor wave at the one-cell stage and a major wave around the eight-cell stage in humans. DUX4, whose expression is promoted by DPPA2 and DPPA4, binds promoters of early embryonic genes such as ZSCAN4, LEUTX, DUXA and KDM4E and recruits coactivators including CREBBP and EP300 to activate them; it also drives bidirectional transcription from endogenous retroviral long terminal repeats and pericentric satellite repeats, the latter contributing to chromocenter formation. Clearance of maternal transcripts by the uridylyltransferases TUT4 and TUT7 accompanies the handover to embryonic control.

MITF-M is the melanocyte-specific master transcription factor, and beyond pigmentation it directs a set of target genes that keep proliferating melanocytes and melanoma cells genomically stable. Through this arm of its programme it drives replication and repair machinery, including the MCM2 and MCM5 subunits of the replicative helicase, the DNA ligase LIG1 that seals nicks during replication and repair, the homologous recombination and damage-response factor BRCA1, and the telomerase catalytic subunit TERT for chromosome end maintenance. Losing MITF by RNA interference allows DNA damage to accumulate and pushes cells into senescence, whereas MITF suppression driven by ATF4 and translational reprogramming produces a reversible cell cycle arrest without senescence. The pathway therefore links lineage identity to replication licensing, genome integrity and proliferative lifespan, and is central to how melanoma cells switch between proliferative and invasive, dedifferentiated states.

The luminal epithelial lineage of the mammary gland comprises the inner cell layer of ducts and the milk-secreting alveolar cells, and it arises postnatally from unipotent luminal progenitors that expand during puberty and pregnancy. This programme builds the ductal tree and the terminal ductal lobular units, and the hormone-receptor-positive and -negative progenitor compartments within it are the presumed cells of origin for major breast cancer subtypes. Fate choice between ductal and alveolar destinies depends on Notch and steroid hormone receptor signalling, while the progenitors retain enough plasticity to revert toward a stem-like state when the microenvironment changes. The epidermal growth factor receptor ligands represented here, amphiregulin, EGF and TGF-alpha, act as the paracrine link between systemic oestrogen signalling and local epithelial proliferation, driving ductal elongation and branching morphogenesis alongside fibroblast growth factor cues that shape duct architecture.

During the branching morphogenesis stage of pancreatic development, committed but still undifferentiated epithelial precursors in the growing ductal tree must be kept proliferating until a subset is released to become hormone-producing endocrine cells. This transcriptional programme sets that balance, and its disruption limits beta cell number, an origin of neonatal diabetes and pancreatic hypoplasia. ONECUT1 sustains expression of ONECUT3 and HNF1B, which maintain the epithelial progenitor state and duct formation, while NEUROG3 induction marks the commitment of individual cells to the endocrine lineage. Notch signalling through NOTCH1, RBPJ and Mastermind-like coactivators, with the acetyltransferases CREBBP, EP300, KAT2A and KAT2B, drives the repressor HES1 to restrain NEUROG3 and hold neighbouring cells as progenitors, so that lateral inhibition rations differentiation across the branching epithelium.

MITF-M is the master switch that turns a neural crest-derived precursor into a melanocyte rather than a neuron or Schwann cell, and control of its expression and activity determines pigmentation, melanoblast migration and survival, and, when deregulated, melanoma behaviour. Before commitment, FOXD3, SOX2 and SNAI2 hold the melanocyte-specific promoter silent, with ZIC1, PAX3 and SOX9 upstream and HDAC1 contributing to relief of repression. In committed melanoblasts PAX3 and SOX10 bind the promoter, reinforced by WNT/beta-catenin with LEF1, endothelin signalling through EDNRB, KIT ligand, and melanocortin input via MC1R and cAMP-driven CREB. Once expressed, MITF-M feeds back to extinguish FOXD3 and SOX2, locking in fate. Its protein output is further tuned by MAPK, GSK3B and AKT phosphorylation, SUMO1/UBE2I conjugation, ubiquitin-mediated turnover, 14-3-3 binding, XPO1-dependent export and SIRT1/CBP-p300 acetylation, which shifts occupancy at differentiation target promoters.

During gastrulation, epiblast cells ingressing through the anterior primitive streak become definitive endoderm, the germ layer that gives rise to the gut tube and its derivative organs including liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung epithelium. Its specification is driven by high NODAL signalling, which acts through SMAD2 and SMAD3 with SMAD4 to induce EOMES, MIXL1 and goosecoid; EOMES in turn switches on FOXA2, SOX17 and the GATA4/GATA6 pair that define endodermal identity and license later organ-specific programmes. Unlike prospective mesoderm, these progenitors retain E-cadherin rather than switching to N-cadherin, avoiding a full epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and instead remodelling adhesion so they can intercalate into an epithelial sheet; CDH1 together with the chemokine receptor CXCR4 is the usual way the population is isolated. WNT input via CTNNB1 and TCF7L2 patterns the streak alongside brachyury. Directing stem cells through this step is the starting point for making hepatocytes and insulin-producing beta cells.

Somitogenesis is the periodic segmentation of the vertebrate embryo's paraxial mesoderm into somites, the blocks of mesenchyme that give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis; its failure produces congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Segment size and spacing arise from a clock-and-wavefront arrangement, in which a molecular oscillator in presomitic mesoderm meets gradients of WNT, FGF and retinoic acid signalling that set the determination front. The oscillator is built from Notch-pathway negative feedback: HES7 represses its own transcription, and the glycosyltransferase LFNG, induced through NOTCH1/RBPJ, feeds back to dampen Notch, with DLL1 and DLL3 ligands shaping the response. At the front, TBX6 and MSGN1 drive MESP2, which turns on EPHA4 for boundary formation and RIPPLY2 to extinguish TBX6. Rapid proteasomal turnover keeps these short-lived regulators oscillating.

The pancreas begins as a pair of buds of endoderm whose cells are already committed to become the exocrine acini, ducts and islets, and this transcriptional programme is what specifies and maintains that early precursor state. Much of it is inferred from mouse embryology, where loss of the founding factors causes pancreatic agenesis or severe hypoplasia; in humans, mutations in the same genes underlie pancreatic and beta-cell developmental disorders, including diabetes arising from failed islet formation. HNF1B, ONECUT1 and PDX1 act in the nascent bud, and together with mesenchymal FGF10 signalling they drive expression of a second tier that includes PTF1A, ONECUT3, NR5A2 and NKX6-1. These downstream factors begin to separate the acinar and endocrine fates, so the network functions as the hierarchical link between endodermal patterning and later hormone- and enzyme-producing cell identity.

Gastrulation converts a single-layered epiblast into the three germ layers, and germ layer formation at this stage sets out the body plan: everything from notochord and heart to gut endoderm traces back to cells that ingress through the primitive streak. NODAL signalling through SMAD2, SMAD3 and SMAD4, with the chromatin reader TRIM33, acts together with BMP4 and WNT-driven beta-catenin/TCF7-LEF1 input to position the streak posteriorly and to switch on the first mesendoderm transcription factors, TBXT and EOMES. These, with FOXH1, MIXL1 and GSC, specify mesoderm and definitive endoderm while shutting down the pluripotency network of POU5F1, SOX2 and NANOG. Mesoderm emerges by epithelial-mesenchymal transition; endoderm uses a partial, more plastic version. Failure of streak formation arrests the embryo before any organ lineage exists.

Between the future brain and the future skin, a strip of ectoderm is set aside that will become the neural crest and the cranial placodes; specifying this neural plate border is what allows vertebrates to build a peripheral nervous system, craniofacial skeleton, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, lens, inner ear and olfactory epithelium. The territory is defined positionally by intermediate levels of BMP and FGF with a graded WNT input, so that BMP4, FGF4 and WNT3A acting through beta-catenin and TCF7L1 place cells between neural and epidermal fates rather than in either. Within that domain a combination of transcription factors, including GBX2, TFAP2A and its paralogues, PAX3, PAX7, MSX1, DLX5 and ZIC1, cross-regulate into a self-reinforcing border identity while pluripotency factors are resolved. No single gene marks the border; failure here underlies neurocristopathies and craniofacial malformation.

The pancreas begins as two buds of foregut endoderm, and this developmental lineage traces how definitive endoderm formed at gastrulation is patterned along the body axes and directed into multipotent pancreatic progenitor cells that will later give rise to acinar, ductal and islet endocrine cells, including insulin-producing beta cells. Dorsal foregut endoderm passes through a duodeno-pancreatic intermediate state and ventral endoderm through a hepato-pancreatic or pancreato-biliary one, with signals from surrounding mesenchyme and notochord deciding pancreatic rather than hepatic or biliary fate. The growth factors here act as those instructive cues: fibroblast growth factors including FGF10 from the mesenchyme sustain progenitor proliferation and expansion of the buds, alongside FGF2, FGF4, FGF7 and EGF. Failure of this specification step underlies pancreatic agenesis and neonatal diabetes, and the same cues are used to make beta cells from stem cells in vitro.

After fertilization the embryo must dismantle the stockpile of messages it inherited from the oocyte, and zygotic decay is the arm of that clearance carried out by factors the zygotic genome itself switches on. Timely removal of maternal transcripts allows the embryo to hand control of gene expression to its own genome; when it fails, transcript levels stay abnormal, development stalls and infertility follows. Mechanistically, partially deadenylated maternal mRNAs held in a closed-loop translation complex with cap-binding and poly(A)-binding proteins are tagged at their 3' ends with untemplated uridines by the terminal uridylyltransferases TUT4 and TUT7, whose expression is induced in the zygote. The uridine tail recruits PABPN1, which in turn brings in the 3'-to-5' exoribonuclease DIS3L2 to destroy the transcript, linking deadenylation, uridylation and exonucleolytic decay into one maternal-to-zygotic transition programme.

The islets of Langerhans arise during development from duct-like bipotent trunk progenitors of the pancreas, and this step describes their passage into a committed endocrine mid-progenitor state that still retains the capacity to make alpha, beta, delta, gamma and epsilon cells. Whether a trunk progenitor takes the ductal or the endocrine route is decided largely by its mechanical environment, which is why the matrix proteins dominate here. Fibronectin and vitronectin engage integrin alpha5beta1, promote cell spreading and sustain a YAP1-NOTCH mechanosignalling axis that represses endocrine commitment, while fibrillar collagens and laminins favour confinement, relieving that repression so NEUROG3 can rise and progenitor markers such as SOX9 and ONECUT1 fall. EGF signalling likewise restrains NEUROG3 induction. Understanding these cues underpins efforts to direct stem cells toward insulin-producing beta cells for diabetes therapy.

The outer skin surface between hair follicles and glands is continuously rebuilt by keratinocytes that move upward through defined layers, and this differentiation programme produces the cornified barrier that blocks pathogen entry and water loss. Stem cells in the basal layer self-renew and generate transit amplifying cells, which divide several times before committing to a spinous, then granular, then corneocyte fate; corneocytes discard nuclei and organelles to become flattened, cross-linked squames that are shed and replaced throughout life. Each transition depends on cues from the surrounding microenvironment, with epidermal growth factor signalling favouring basal proliferation and delaying commitment, so that the balance between renewal and terminal differentiation sets epidermal thickness and turnover. Disruption of this balance underlies barrier-defective skin disease, impaired wound repair, and keratinocyte-derived tumours.

Growth factor and insulin signalling suppresses a stress- and starvation-driven transcriptional programme, and AKT-mediated inactivation of FOXO1A is the step that accomplishes it. In the absence of signalling, FOXO1 shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm with enough nuclear residence to drive genes for gluconeogenesis, autophagy, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis; once insulin or growth factors activate the AKT isoforms downstream of PI3K, the kinases phosphorylate FOXO1 at several sites, promoting 14-3-3 binding and its exclusion from the nucleus, so the programme is switched off. This is the branch of insulin action that lowers hepatic glucose output and permits growth and survival, and its loss of control contributes to insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia. Because FOXO1 restrains proliferation, constitutive AKT activity in tumours keeps this tumour-suppressive factor cytoplasmic and inert.

The melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, in its melanocyte-specific M isoform, does more than drive pigmentation: it sets how mobile and invasive a melanocytic cell is. Through targets such as the adhesion molecule CEACAM1, the actin-nucleating formin DIAPH1 and the purine-metabolic enzyme GMPR, MITF tunes cell-cell adhesion and the state of the actin cytoskeleton, and it also feeds into epithelial-mesenchymal-transition programmes via SNAI2. This matters most in melanoma, where cells switch between an MITF-high proliferative, differentiated state and an MITF-low invasive state; the level of MITF activity therefore helps determine whether tumour cells divide locally or migrate and metastasise, and it influences response to targeted therapy. The same transcriptional control underlies normal melanoblast migration during development, linking lineage identity to motility rather than treating them as separate programmes.

The melanocyte master regulator MITF-M does not simply promote growth; its target gene output shifts with its own activity level, and the cell cycle genes it controls explain why. At intermediate activity MITF drives proliferation by inducing mitotic and G1/S machinery including CDK2, cyclin D1, cyclin B1, CDC25B and PLK1, plus the receptor tyrosine kinase MET; when activity falls, cells dedifferentiate, slow their cycle and become invasive, and when it rises too far the CDK inhibitors p21 and p16 impose arrest. This rheostat behaviour is central to melanocyte biology and to melanoma, where phenotype switching between proliferative and invasive states tracks MITF levels independently of pigmentation output. Wnt-responsive TCF/LEF factors with beta-catenin feed into the same promoters, while TBX2 and the SIN3A-HDAC1 corepressor set the repressive side of the balance.

Mammary glands arise from non-neural surface ectoderm, and the mammary stem cells derived from that ectoderm are the founders of the ductal tree, capable of regenerating a functional gland and of giving rise to both luminal and myoepithelial progeny. This developmental lineage traces that transition, from embryonic surface ectoderm to basal-residing mammary stem cells (also described as bipotent progenitors), which in the adult human breast are rare and concentrated in the ducts of terminal ductal lobular units. Their behaviour underlies placode and bud formation, pubertal ductal outgrowth, pregnancy-associated remodelling, and, when misregulated, the stem-like compartments implicated in breast cancer. FGF10 signalling through its epithelial receptor is one of the better-conserved inputs generating and maintaining these cells, acting alongside Wnt/beta-catenin, Hedgehog, Notch and ovarian hormone signalling in mammary specification.

Sperm package nearly all of their DNA with protamines rather than histones, achieving extreme compaction at the cost of a transcriptionally silent, epigenetically bare genome. Immediately after fertilization the male pronucleus must be rebuilt into ordinary chromatin using histones supplied by the oocyte, and this protamine-to-nucleosome exchange is what makes the paternal genome decondense, become permissive for transcription, and participate in the first embryonic divisions. The kinase SRPK1 phosphorylates PRM1 and PRM2, which promotes their removal by nucleoplasmin NPM2 and recruits the histone chaperone HIRA; HIRA then deposits the replacement-independent variant H3.3 together with core H2B and H4 histones, H2AX, and the oocyte-specific linker histone H1-8. Arginine methylation of H3.3 by METTL23 supports its incorporation. The reprogrammed chromatin established here sets the paternal epigenome inherited by the embryo, and defects contribute to fertilization failure.

The melanocyte transcription factor MITF-M is best known for driving pigmentation genes, but it also runs a second programme that builds and acidifies the degradative compartments of the cell. Its targets here are essentially the whole vacuolar H+-ATPase, both the membrane-embedded V0 sector and the cytosolic V1 ATP-hydrolysing sector, plus an accessory subunit; together these pump protons to acidify lysosomes and endosomes, which is a precondition for hydrolase activity, cargo degradation, receptor recycling and melanosome maturation. The same output supports autophagic flux when melanoma cells are starved of nutrients, giving them a route to recycle their own material and survive stress. MITF also induces the lysosomal acid ceramidase ASAH1, which clears ceramide and thereby links sphingolipid handling to proliferation and drug resistance in melanoma. This places lysosome biogenesis alongside differentiation in the MITF-controlled repertoire.

Circulating monocytes arise in the bone marrow from myeloid progenitors, egress to the blood in a CCR2-dependent manner, and survive there only a day or two before either dying or entering tissues to become monocyte-derived macrophages and dendritic cells. Their differentiation sustains innate defence: classical CD14-high monocytes phagocytose and kill bacteria, non-classical CD16-high monocytes patrol the vasculature and respond to nucleic acids and viruses, with an intermediate antigen-presenting state between them. The two cytokines represented here set the fate and tone of this output: macrophage colony-stimulating factor drives survival, proliferation and mononuclear phagocyte differentiation through its receptor CSF1R, while interferon gamma from T and NK cells licenses classical activation, raising antigen presentation and antimicrobial capacity. Too little of this axis leaves monocyte and macrophage compartments depleted; excess drives the inflammatory monocyte influx seen in atherosclerosis, autoimmunity and chronic infection.

The nephron is the filtering and reabsorbing unit of the kidney, running from glomerulus through proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal segments to the collecting duct, and its formation during fetal life sets the number of nephrons a person will ever have. Nephron development begins where ureteric bud tips meet metanephric mesenchyme: WNT9B from the bud induces progenitors to aggregate and express WNT4, driving a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into renal vesicles, while a self-renewing progenitor pool is maintained in parallel. The vesicle is polarized from the outset, with WT1 acting proximally to repress PAX2 and permit podocyte formation, and LHX1 and POU3F3 specifying distal segments and loop elongation. HNF1B then activates Notch components DLL1, JAG1 and LFNG plus IRX1/IRX2 as the comma- and S-shaped bodies form, and HNF4A supports proximal tubule identity. Defective versions of this programme underlie congenital kidney malformation and reduced nephron endowment.

Pancreatic endocrine cells arise from a transient population of progenitors that switch on neurogenin 3, and this transcriptional programme is what commits those cells away from duct and acinar fates toward the hormone-producing islet lineages. Without it no beta, alpha, delta or PP cells form; loss-of-function mutations in humans cause congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea with permanent neonatal diabetes, and the same programme is the target of efforts to make beta cells from stem cells. NEUROG3 acts as a short-lived pioneer factor that directly induces a second tier of regulators, including PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and the zinc-finger factor INSM1, which together consolidate endocrine identity, drive exit from the cell cycle, and bias progenitors toward particular hormone subtypes. The pathway illustrates how a brief pulse of one factor is converted into a stable differentiated state.

Skin, hair and eye colour depend on a melanocyte transcriptional programme driven by the M-isoform of MITF, which switches on the enzymes and structural proteins that build and move melanosomes. Loss of this output causes hypopigmentation and deafness syndromes, while its reactivation sustains the differentiated state of melanoma cells. MITF binds M-box elements in the promoters of the melanin-synthetic enzymes tyrosinase, TYRP1 and DCT, and of melanosome components such as MLANA, PMEL and GPR143; it also drives RAB27A, MYO5A and melanophilin, the machinery that tethers and transports pigment granules toward the cell periphery for transfer to keratinocytes. Transcription requires partners and coactivators — SOX10, TFAP2A, LEF1 with beta-catenin, CREB1, IRF4 — and remodelling of target promoters by BAF/SWI-SNF chromatin complexes, linking pigmentation gene expression to Wnt and stress-kinase signalling inputs.

The intermediate mesoderm is the strip of embryonic mesoderm that gives rise to the entire urogenital system — gonads, nephric ducts, ureteric epithelium and metanephric mesenchyme — so its specification determines whether kidneys and reproductive tracts form at all, and defects here underlie renal agenesis and urogenital malformation. It is carved out along the medial-lateral axis by graded BMP signalling, high in lateral plate and low in paraxial mesoderm, while Wnt, FGF and retinoic acid gradients set its position along the head-to-tail axis. OSR1 and LHX1 mark the territory first, followed by the paralogous transcription factors PAX2 and PAX8, which act in a mutually reinforcing loop with the earlier factors. FOXC1 and FOXC2 expressed in neighbouring paraxial mesoderm repress LHX1 and OSR1 and so confine the domain. The same cues are used to direct human pluripotent stem cells toward kidney lineages in vitro.

Early in development the dorsal epiblast thickens into the neural plate, the sheet that folds into the neural tube and becomes the entire central nervous system; incomplete closure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Formation of the posterior neural plate specifies the caudal half of that sheet, which gives rise to the hindbrain and anterior spinal cord, and it is built differently from the anterior half: rather than arising directly from epiblast, its caudal portion derives from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors in which WNT and FGF signalling, via WNT3A and FGF8, drive SOX2 through a dedicated posterior enhancer while TBX6 pulls sister cells toward paraxial mesoderm. Regional identity is then fixed by mutual transcriptional repression between GBX2 posteriorly and OTX2 anteriorly, setting the midbrain-hindbrain boundary, with SOX1, ZEB2 and POU3F1 accompanying commitment to neural fate.

The kidney and much of the male reproductive tract descend from a single epithelial tube, and this pathway covers how that nephric duct is carved out of intermediate mesoderm. Cells of the nephrogenic cord epithelialise in response to signals from adjacent somites and surface ectoderm, forming the duct of the pronephros and then the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, from whose caudal end the ureteric bud emerges to branch into the adult metanephric kidney. Positional cues from retinoic acid acting via HOXB4 set where this occurs, while PAX2 and PAX8 with LHX1 mark early renal progenitors; LHX1 and GATA3 sustain each other in a self-reinforcing loop that drives duct differentiation and switches on targets such as EMX2, ID4, nephronectin and the receptor tyrosine kinase RET. RET responds to GDNF from metanephric mesenchyme, and nephronectin engages integrin alpha8beta1, coupling duct to mesenchyme. Failure here produces renal agenesis and other congenital urinary tract anomalies.

Pancreatic ductal cells form the single-layered epithelium that lines the branching duct tree and carries acinar secretions and bicarbonate to the gut; their developmental lineage traces back through bipotent trunk progenitors, which also yield endocrine progenitors, to the multipotent pancreatic progenitors of the early bud. Duct shape changes with calibre, from cuboidal to high columnar, and apical cilia and microvilli mark the mature cell. The genes here are the matrix side of that programme: fibrillar collagens together with fibronectin and vitronectin build the interstitial stroma around growing ducts, while the laminin chains and their assembled trimers, with collagen IV-type partners, form the basement membrane that polarises the epithelium and positions trunk progenitors for duct versus endocrine choice. Adhesion to this matrix via integrin engagement guides branching morphogenesis, and disturbed duct identity underlies cystic disease and ductal adenocarcinoma with its dense desmoplastic matrix.

The permanent kidney begins when a single outgrowth, the ureteric bud, sprouts from the nephric (Wolffian) duct into the adjacent metanephric mesenchyme; that bud goes on to form the ureter, branches to build the collecting duct tree, and induces nephrons at its tips. Getting the number and position of buds right determines final nephron endowment, and errors produce renal agenesis, duplex or multicystic dysplastic kidneys and other congenital urinary tract anomalies. Budding depends on reciprocal signalling: nephronectin secreted by the duct engages integrin alpha8/beta1 on the mesenchyme to switch on GDNF, which acts through the RET receptor tyrosine kinase and its co-receptor GFRA1 on duct cells and induces WNT11. Transcription factors including PAX2, EYA1, SIX1/SIX2, SALL1 and posterior HOX11 paralogues specify the competent mesenchyme, while SLIT2-ROBO2, BMP4 with its antagonist gremlin, and FOXC1/FOXC2 restrict budding to one site.
